content: FATE1, also known as Fetal and Adult Testis-Expressed 1, is a protein encoded by the FATE1 gene in humans. It has been identified as a cancer-testis antigen (CTA) in hepatocellular carcinomas, as well as in gastric and colon cancers. During fetal development, FATE1 expression is specific to the testis, particularly between 6 and 11 weeks of gestation. In adults, its expression is predominantly localized to the testis and adrenal glands, with lower levels of expression observed in the lungs, heart, kidneys, and throughout the brain. FATE1 belongs to the Miff protein family. Its C-terminal domain contains a transmembrane domain and a coiled-coil domain, which exhibit significant structural similarity to the mitochondrial fission factor (MFF) protein. MFF is known to play a role in mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission processes. The FATE1 gene is located on the long arm of the X chromosome at region 28, spanning base pairs 150,884,502 to 150,891,617. It has been hypothesized that FATE1 utilizes its C-terminal transmembrane domain to anchor itself to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Simultaneously, its C-terminal coiled-coil domain interacts with mitochondria. FATE1 is localized to mitochondria-associated ER membranes (MAMs), where it modulates the distance between the ER and mitochondria. This regulation influences calcium (Ca²⁺)-dependent and drug-dependent apoptosis in cancer cells. FATE1 expression reduces mitochondrial calcium uptake, which in turn decreases mitochondrial fragmentation associated with calcium uptake. This mechanism provides protection against cell death. FATE1 is detectable in all tumor-derived cell lines but is either low or undetectable in telomere-immortalized, non-tumorigenic fibroblasts and lung epithelial cells. It is considered essential for the survival of tumor cells, as depletion of FATE1 reduces cell viability in melanoma, breast, prostate, and sarcoma cancer models. Upregulation of FATE1 is mediated by the transcription factor steroidogenic factor-1 (SF-1), which is involved in adrenal and gonadal development as well as adrenocortical carcinoma. This upregulation increases the ER-mitochondria distance and is exploited by cancer cells to functionally uncouple the ER and mitochondria. Silencing the FATE1 gene sensitizes non-small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC) cell lines to paclitaxel, a chemotherapeutic drug used to treat various cancers. Elevated levels of FATE1 are associated with higher mortality rates in colorectal cancers. However, in NSCLC, increased FATE1 expression alone does not reduce survival rates. A decrease in survival is observed only when FATE1 elevation is accompanied by increased expression of RNF183.
